title: Frances Tiafoe and Francisco Cerúndolo win biggest titles of their careers as Wimbledon approaches
content:
On Sunday afternoon, Frances Tiafoe and Francisco Cerúndolo won the biggest titles of their careers.

It had figured to be a golden day for American men when Tiafoe was taking control of the Halle Open final in Germany against compatriot Taylor Fritz, just as Tommy Paul went up a set and a break of serve against Argentina’s Cerúndolo at Queen’s, in west London.

When both matches were over, Tiafoe was holding his fourth ATP Tour trophy after overwhelming and outplaying Fritz, his good friend, 6-4, 6-4 in front of a raucous crowd in Halle. Paul, though could not get over the line. Cerúndolo, who spent the majority of the match as the better player, while being worse in its most important moments, flipped that script to win 6-7, 6-4, 6-3.

Tiafoe’s title capped off quite a week for the 28-year-old, who suffered a heart-breaking loss to Italy’s Matteo Arnaldi at the French Open just shy of three weeks ago. In Halle, he beat more than one top-10 player during one tournament for the first time, taking down three in all — Flavio Cobolli, Félix Auger-Aliassime and Fritz. He saved match points in the quarterfinal against Auger-Aliassime, and the win over French Open finalist Cobolli was an impressive one. Against Fritz, he glided to victory.

“I lost a lot of 500 finals, I lost a lot of finals in my career, this is big,” Tiafoe said in quotes circulated by the ATP. After calling the loss to then-world No. 104 Arnaldi “one of the toughest losses of my career,” he described how he rode an immaculate service day to the title in Halle.

“I felt I couldn’t miss one and I returned really well,” he said. “I played a clean match. I had to.”

Most importantly for Tiafoe, he is rounding into form at just the right time for him. He gets fired up for Wimbledon, the U.S. Open and the D.C. Open in his home city of Washington, D.C. He has said that he can struggle to find motivation the rest of the year.

After a sobering U.S. Open defeat to Germany’s Jan-Lennard Struff in 2025, and a subsequent, even more sobering meeting with his closest confidantes in which they told him not to waste his and their time, he has tried to apply himself more consistently. With the win, Tiafoe returns to the top 20.

For a while, Paul looked like he was going to follow Tiafoe into the winners’ circle. Paul won Queen’s in 2024 and missed the 2025 edition due to injury, so he was going for a second title in as many appearances, and like Tiafoe, he could have used a title. Paul suffered his own nightmarish exit from the French Open, losing to Casper Ruud from two sets up in the third round.

Instead, Paul grew a little tight on important points just as Cerúndolo, who had spent most of the match in that state, started to loosen up a little. Paul got passive, missed first serves and gave a player with one of the fiercest forehands in the game too many short balls on that wing.

And while the American saved four championship points — three of them on his serve — Cerúndolo worked a point around to an overhead on the fifth to win his first ATP 500 title, and a second title on grass. His first, at the 2023 Eastbourne Open in England, also came against Paul.

“We always seem to have unreal matches and today you were the better player,” Paul, 29 said of Cerúndolo, 27, in the trophy ceremony. The Argentine celebrated his win in the presence of his father — on Father’s Day in both the U.K. and Argentina — and another milestone made it extra special.

“It’s the first time my dad has taken a flight and the first time he has come to watch me outside of Argentina,” Cerúndolo said, just after lifting the trophy.
